_about: Guided study content. Teaching text is editorial - it is this app's own words and is never Scripture. Not one word of Scripture lives in this file: lessons name references, and scripture:build resolves them against the same pinned WEB corpus the daily readings come from, then emits canonical ids. A reference here that the corpus cannot resolve fails the build.

rules: Ground every explanation in the passage and the context actually read, and list that context in 'basis'.
Explain what the passage says and what a reader needs to know to follow it. Do not add promises, history or doctrine the passage does not carry.
Where a reading is genuinely disputed, state it conservatively or keep it off the centre of the lesson.
Never tell a reader that God selected this lesson for them.
Teach something. Avoiding all interpretation produces a lesson that is safe and useless.

studies.title: New to the Bible
studies.summary: What this collection actually is, the story it tells, and where to begin reading.
studies.audience: Someone opening it for the first time, or coming back after a long gap.

lessons.title: What kind of book this is
lessons.understand:
The Bible is not one book. It is a collection of writings from different times and in different forms — histories, letters, poems, songs, legal codes — brought together as Scripture.

Luke's opening shows what that means in practice. He is a named author writing to a named reader. He says others have already written accounts, that he looked into things himself, and that he is setting them down in order for a stated reason: so that Theophilus can know how reliable the things he was taught really are.

That is a useful expectation to begin with. You are not opening a single argument. You are opening a library, and each piece has an author, an audience and a purpose. Knowing which kind of writing you are in front of changes how you read it.
lessons.lookCloser: Luke says he wrote so his reader could know the certainty of what he had been taught. What does that suggest about the kind of confidence he expected reading to produce?
lessons.reflect: What made you want to open the Bible? Write it down before you begin — it is worth having later.

lessons.title: The story it tells
lessons.understand:
These two passages are separated by the whole of the Bible — the first line of the first book, and a few paragraphs from the end of the last.

Read together they show that the collection has a shape. It opens with God making a world. It closes with God living among people in a world made new, with grief and death gone. Everything in between sits somewhere on that line: what went wrong, what was promised, and what was done about it.

This matters for a beginner because the Bible is easy to read as disconnected fragments — a rule here, a story there, a verse on a card. The individual parts are far easier to place once you know the collection is going somewhere, and where.
lessons.lookCloser: One passage describes a beginning and the other an ending. What is present in both?
lessons.reflect: Which end of that story is easier for you to believe today — the beginning, or the end?

lessons.title: Who Jesus is
lessons.understand:
John opens his account of Jesus by echoing the first words of Genesis — "In the beginning". He is placing Jesus before the creation rather than inside it.

"The Word" translates a Greek term his first readers would have met in discussions of the reason or order behind the world. John takes that familiar idea and does something unexpected with it: the Word is not a principle but someone — who was with God, who was God, and through whom everything was made.

Then verse 14 makes the claim the rest of the book rests on: the one John has been describing did not remain outside the world he made, but took on a human life within it. John is not describing a teacher whose reputation grew after his death. He is claiming that God's own self-expression arrived in a body, and that people saw it.
lessons.lookCloser: Why do you think John chose to open with Jesus as "the Word", rather than with his birth or his teaching?
lessons.reflect: Before today, who did you understand Jesus to be?

lessons.title: What the good news says
lessons.understand:
"Gospel" is an old word meaning good news, and the first passage is the New Testament's own earliest summary of it. Paul says he is handing on something he himself received, which means these lines were already in circulation before he wrote them down.

The summary is short and factual: Christ died for our sins, he was buried, he was raised, and he was seen. Paul then lists people who saw him, several by name, and notes that most of them were still alive — an odd detail to include unless he expected readers to be able to ask them.

The second passage says what this news asks of you, and what it does not. It is described as a gift received rather than a wage earned. The reason given is not that effort is worthless, but that a gift leaves nobody with grounds to boast.
lessons.lookCloser: Paul names witnesses and points out that most were still living. What kind of claim is he making by adding that detail?
lessons.reflect: Which is harder to accept — that the news is true, or that it is free?

lessons.title: How to begin reading
lessons.understand:
Luke describes a group in Beroea who heard Paul preach and then went and checked. They are called more noble for it — not for agreeing quickly, but for receiving eagerly and examining daily to see whether it was so. Testing what you are told is treated here as a credit, not a failure of faith.

The psalm supplies the other half. A lamp at your feet lights the next step, not the whole road. That is a realistic picture of what reading Scripture usually feels like: enough to move by, rarely enough to see the entire route at once.

So begin somewhere concrete rather than at page one. A Gospel is the usual advice, and Luke — whose opening you read in the first lesson — is a reasonable place to start. Read a section rather than a single line.
lessons.lookCloser: The Beroeans examined daily rather than once. What would change if you treated reading as something returned to rather than finished?
lessons.reflect: What is one question you want to keep asking as you read?

studies.title: Who is Jesus?
studies.summary: Who the Gospels say Jesus is, from the promise that came before him to the call he makes on anyone who follows.
studies.audience: Anyone who wants to know what Christians actually claim about Jesus, whether or not they believe it.

lessons.title: The one who was expected
lessons.understand:
Jesus does not arrive in the Gospels as a surprise. He arrives into a people who had been waiting a long time, and the shape of that waiting explains a great deal about what followed.

Isaiah wrote to a nation living under threat, and the promise he gives them is oddly domestic. It is a child. But the titles pile up past anything a child could carry, and the throne named is David’s — the royal line God had promised would not run out.

Centuries later, Luke describes an angel telling a young woman in an unremarkable town that her son will be given that same throne, and that his reign will have no end.

Whatever else the Gospels are doing, they are placing Jesus inside a promise that was already old. The first Christians did not claim he had founded a new religion. They claimed he was what an old one had been waiting for.
lessons.lookCloser: Both passages describe a reign that does not end. What else do the two have in common?
lessons.reflect: Does it change anything to meet Jesus as the answer to a long wait rather than as a new idea?

lessons.title: God’s own likeness, in a human life
lessons.understand:
The letter to the Hebrews opens by comparing two kinds of speech. God had spoken before — through prophets, in pieces, across centuries. Then, the writer says, he spoke again, and this time the message was a person.

That is a larger claim than it sounds. A prophet carries words on God’s behalf. A son is not a delivery method; he carries the family likeness. Hebrews presses exactly there: to look at the Son is to see what God is like, not approximately but exactly.

Two details are easy to read past. The Son is described as holding creation together, so this is not a figure who enters the story late. And after dealing with sin, he sits down. Priests stood at their work, because the work was never finished. Sitting is the posture of someone whose task is complete.
lessons.lookCloser: The passage lists several things the Son does. Which happen before a human life, and which after?
lessons.reflect: If Jesus is meant to show what God is like, how does that compare with the picture you already carry?

lessons.title: The announcement he came making
lessons.understand:
Mark compresses Jesus’ message into one sentence, and what is missing from it matters. There is no instruction, no doctrine, no programme. There is news — that the waiting is over and God’s reign has arrived — and then an invitation to turn around and trust it.

The word kingdom misleads a modern reader, who hears a place. It is closer to a rule actively arriving: what things look like where God is genuinely in charge.

Luke shows the same claim made in a specific room. Jesus reads aloud from Isaiah about someone anointed to bring good news to the poor and freedom to prisoners, hands the scroll back, sits down, and says it has happened today.

Read Isaiah’s sentence to its end and it carries on into judgement. Jesus stops before that clause. What he announces first is release.
lessons.lookCloser: Make a list of what Jesus says he was sent to do. Who are the people named in it?
lessons.reflect: What changes if this is treated as news rather than as advice?

lessons.title: Power that stops for one person
lessons.understand:
Two kinds of power sit side by side here, and the pairing is the lesson.

The first scene is small. A man whose skin disease has cut him off from ordinary human contact does not ask whether Jesus is able to heal him. He asks whether Jesus is willing. Jesus answers first by touching him, which under the law of the time was the one thing nobody did, and then by saying that he is.

The second scene is enormous. A storm that frightens experienced fishermen stops because he tells it to. And the men who have just been rescued end up more afraid afterwards than they were during it.

Their question closes the scene, and it is the question this study is named for. Mark does not answer it. He lets the two scenes stand together: whatever this authority is, it is the kind that stops for one desperate man.
lessons.lookCloser: The man asks about willingness rather than ability. How does the reply answer both?
lessons.reflect: Which is harder to believe — that Jesus could help, or that he would want to?

lessons.title: Why he died
lessons.understand:
Jesus explains his own death before it happens, and he does it in the middle of an argument about rank. His followers want position. He tells them greatness runs the other way, then offers himself as the example — not a leader who serves, but one whose life is handed over for other people.

The word translated ransom carries the sense of a price paid to release someone. Christians have explained how that works in more than one way, and the New Testament uses several images for it. The claim in the passage is narrower and firmer: his death does something for others. It is not merely something done to him.

Isaiah’s poem, far older, describes a figure who suffers in the place of others. The earliest Christians read it as a description of Jesus. In Acts, a man reading this poem asks whether the prophet means himself or someone else, and is told about Jesus.
lessons.lookCloser: Isaiah’s lines move between “he” and “we”. Trace which words belong to which.
lessons.reflect: What difference does it make whether his death was a defeat or something he intended?

lessons.title: The claim that he was raised
lessons.understand:
Luke tells this scene like a man expecting to be doubted.

The disciples’ first thought is that they are seeing a ghost, and Luke says so plainly. He does not present them as people primed to believe. He presents them as frightened, unconvinced, and — in one memorable phrase — unable to accept the news because it is too good.

The evidence he then offers is stubbornly physical. Hands and feet. An invitation to touch. Bones, which a spirit does not have. Finally a piece of cooked fish, eaten in front of them.

Whatever a reader concludes about it, it is worth being clear what is being claimed. Not that Jesus survived. Not that his memory endured, or that his friends went on feeling his presence. The claim is that an executed man was alive again, in a body, and hungry.
lessons.lookCloser: Count the ways Luke shows this is a body rather than a vision.
lessons.reflect: The first witnesses doubted. Does it help or hinder you that their doubt was written down?

lessons.title: What following him costs
lessons.understand:
The setting matters. Moments earlier Peter has said out loud that Jesus is the Messiah, and Jesus has answered by describing his own rejection and death. Only then does he turn to the crowd and say what following him will involve.

Carrying a cross has softened into a phrase for putting up with hardship. It did not mean that. A cross was an execution, and the people listening had seen them used. He is describing a life no longer arranged around self-protection.

Then he states the exchange, and it lands as an observation rather than a threat: gripping your life is precisely how you lose it. What he offers is not a better life in the ordinary sense. It is a different kind of one, and he says the price out loud before anyone agrees to it.

That refusal to undersell is itself part of the answer to who he is.
lessons.lookCloser: The words life and save each appear more than once, and not always meaning the same thing. Which is which?
lessons.reflect: What would it look like to arrange a life around something other than protecting it?

studies.title: Understanding the Gospel
studies.summary: What Christians mean by the word gospel, followed through Scripture from a good creation to a life remade.
studies.audience: Anyone who has heard the word for years without having it explained, or had it explained too fast.

lessons.title: A world made on purpose
lessons.understand:
Most short accounts of the Christian message open with what has gone wrong. Genesis opens earlier, and the order matters: before there is anything to rescue, there is something worth rescuing.

Two claims sit in these lines. The first is that people are made in God’s image. The text never explains what that likeness consists of, and Christians have discussed it for centuries — but it does something more immediate. It assigns a standing. Dignity here is not achieved and not handed out by merit. It is given, and given to everyone in view, without qualification.

The second is the verdict at the end of the day’s work. Not adequate. Not acceptable. Very good.

Hold both, because everything that follows depends on them. What comes next in this story is a tear in something that was good to start with, which is why it reads as loss rather than as the way things always were.
lessons.lookCloser: Who is included in what is said about God’s image, and who is left out?
lessons.reflect: If human dignity is given rather than earned, what would follow from taking that seriously?

lessons.title: The hiding
lessons.understand:
Notice what comes first. Not a thunderbolt. A couple hiding among the trees, and a God who comes looking and asks where they are.

That is this book’s picture of what has gone wrong, and it is more relational than legal. The damage surfaces as fear, concealment, and a new distance between people and the God who made them. Sin here is not primarily a list of infractions. It is a relationship broken from one side.

Paul, writing far later, refuses to let anyone stand outside the problem. Everyone falls short. The aim is not to induce shame; it is to remove the ranking, because there is no group in the room that does not need help.

And he does not stop at the diagnosis. The same sentence runs on into a gift. Christians often use the word justified for this — being put right with God freely, because of Christ, rather than because the account was eventually balanced.
lessons.lookCloser: God asks a question. What does the man’s answer reveal about what has changed between them?
lessons.reflect: What do people tend to do with the parts of themselves they would rather not have seen?

lessons.title: God’s move toward us
lessons.understand:
Between the hiding in Genesis and the arrival of Jesus lies most of the Bible, and it is tempting to read those centuries as a delay. They read better as the rescue already under way.

God’s answer to a broken world is neither to abandon it nor to repair it on the spot. He calls one man out of one country and makes him a short list of promises. Land. Descendants. A name.

But the promise does not stop with Abram, and the last line is the one to watch. The blessing is aimed outward, at every family on earth. Whatever else this nation’s story becomes, it begins with a stated intention to reach past itself.

Paul later points at this exact sentence and calls it the good news announced ahead of time. On that reading, what happens in Jesus is not a change of plan. It is an old promise being kept.
lessons.lookCloser: Count the promises made to Abram. Which of them rest on him, and which on God?
lessons.reflect: What is the difference between a God who fixes the world instantly and one who works through a long history?

lessons.title: The cross, and who it was for
lessons.understand:
Paul is arguing about timing, and the weight of it rests on a single word: while.

He sets the comparison up carefully. People do occasionally die for someone worth dying for; a genuinely good person might inspire it. That, he says, is roughly the outer limit of ordinary human love — and even there, the one being died for has to be worth it.

Then he puts the cross outside that limit. Christ died for people who were not worth it and had not asked. Not once they improved. Not after they had made themselves presentable. While.

How the cross achieves what it achieves has been discussed for as long as there have been Christians, and the New Testament reaches for several images. Paul’s concern in these three verses is narrower. He is using the timing to show what kind of love this is: love that moves first, toward people who have given it no reason to.
lessons.lookCloser: Paul describes the people Christ died for three times, using three different words. What are they?
lessons.reflect: What changes if love arrived before there was anything in you to reward?

lessons.title: Why the resurrection is not optional
lessons.understand:
It would be easy to treat the resurrection as a happy ending fastened onto the important part. Paul refuses that arrangement, and he does it by saying out loud what follows if it never happened.

Read what he is prepared to concede. If Christ was not raised, faith is empty, forgiveness has not occurred, the Christian dead are simply dead, and believers are the most pitiable people alive. He reaches for no fallback — not that the teaching is still wise, not that the community is still worthwhile. He lets the whole thing stand or fall on an event.

Then comes the turn, and one phrase carries it. First fruit is a harvest word. The first sheaf is not the point of a harvest; it is the evidence that the rest of the field is coming.

So the claim is not only that one man was raised. It is that his rising has opened something meant to include others.
lessons.lookCloser: Paul lists what would be true if Christ were not raised. How many separate consequences does he name?
lessons.reflect: Paul stakes everything on an event rather than on the value of the teaching. Why might that matter?

lessons.title: Grace, and the life that follows
lessons.understand:
Two words hold this passage together, and their order is the entire point.

The first is gift. Paul’s language is pointedly financial in what it rules out: not wages, not achievement, nothing anyone could invoice for. He presses further than most summaries dare — the people being rescued are called dead, and death is not a condition that contributes to its own recovery.

The second is workmanship. Having ruled out earning, Paul does not conclude that behaviour has stopped mattering. He says the reverse. Good works are not the price of the rescue; they are what the rescued life is for, and he pictures them as already prepared, waiting to be walked into.

This is where the shortest summaries of the Christian message usually fail. What is described here is not an arrangement for securing a destination. It is a person made alive now, for a life with a shape to it.
lessons.lookCloser: Find the two things Paul says this rescue does not come by, and the one thing he says it is for.
lessons.reflect: If good works follow the gift rather than pay for it, what does that change about trying to live well?

studies.title: Learning to Pray
studies.summary: What prayer is in Scripture, how Jesus taught it, and how to begin — including what to do when nothing seems to come back.
studies.audience: Anyone who wants to pray and is unsure how to start, or who started once and stopped.

lessons.title: What prayer actually is
lessons.understand:
Jesus starts by clearing away two mistakes, and both are still with us.

The first is prayer as performance. He describes people praying where they are certain to be seen, and observes — dryly — that they have already got what they came for. His remedy is almost comically plain: shut the door.

The second is prayer as word-count, as though God responded to volume the way a reluctant official responds to persistence. His reason for dismissing that is the surprising part: your Father already knows what you need.

Which could sound like an argument for not bothering. It is the opposite. If prayer is not how God gets informed, then it was never a transaction, and the anxiety about phrasing it correctly falls away. The psalm supplies the picture: pour it out. Not compose it. Not perform it. Pour.
lessons.lookCloser: Jesus names two habits to avoid and gives a reason for each. What are the two reasons?
lessons.reflect: Which of these two mistakes is closer to your own instinct about prayer?

lessons.title: The prayer he gave them
lessons.understand:
Asked for a model, Jesus gives one short enough to memorise, and its shape teaches as much as its wording.

Look at the order. Three lines about God come before anything about the person praying — his name, his reign, his will. Whatever else this is, it is not a form for submitting requests. It begins by getting the room the right way round.

Then the asking, and it is modest. Bread for today, not security for the year. Forgiveness, with a clause attached that ought to slow anyone down, since it ties the receiving to the giving. Protection from testing and from evil.

One detail is easy to miss. Every request is plural. Our bread, our debts, deliver us. Even prayed alone in a shut room, this is not a private arrangement.
lessons.lookCloser: Three requests concern God and three concern the people praying. Where exactly does it turn?
lessons.reflect: The prayer puts God’s concerns before its own. What would it take to pray in that order?

lessons.title: Honest prayer
lessons.understand:
Four times in two verses, the same question: how long. The psalm accuses God of forgetting and of hiding his face. It is not polite, and nobody edited it out. It sits in the collection Israel actually used for worship.

That placement is worth pausing over. If this is in the prayer book, then complaint is not a failure of prayer. It is a form of prayer, and a permitted one. Whatever honesty before God costs, it does not cost admission.

Then the psalm turns, and how it turns matters. The writer says he trusts, that his heart is glad, that he will sing. Read those closing lines again and notice what is absent. Nothing says the enemy left. Nothing reports that the situation resolved.

The turn is not relief arriving. It is a decision made while still waiting, which is a far more usable model than the alternative.
lessons.lookCloser: The psalm changes direction near the end. What has changed by that point, and what has not?
lessons.reflect: What would change if prayer had room for the kind of bluntness this psalm uses?

lessons.title: Asking, and the answer that was no
lessons.understand:
This is the passage to keep when prayer appears not to work.

In the garden, Jesus asks to be spared what is coming. He does not phrase it cautiously; he says plainly that God is able to do it. And the answer is no.

That fact deserves its full weight. If prayer were a dependable mechanism for obtaining outcomes, this prayer would have worked. Whatever unanswered prayer means, it cannot mean the one praying lacked faith or asked badly.

Notice the order, too. He asks for what he genuinely wants, fully, and only then yields. Surrender does not replace the request; it follows it. A prayer that starts out already resigned has skipped a step he did not skip.

Paul writes about anxiety and prayer, and it repays reading precisely. What he promises is not the outcome requested. It is peace — described as something that guards a person, which is language for what holds when circumstances do not.
lessons.lookCloser: Jesus states what God is able to do and what he himself wants. How does his last sentence hold both?
lessons.reflect: How does it sit with you that Jesus asked for something and did not receive it?

lessons.title: Prayer in an ordinary week
lessons.understand:
Luke gives one sentence to Jesus’ prayer habit, and its placement does the work. The crowds are growing. The demand is rising. That is the moment Luke chooses to mention he kept going off alone to pray.

Not that he found time. That he withdrew — deliberately, and repeatedly. Prayer here is not what is left over at the end of a day; it is defended against the day.

Paul’s instruction sounds impossible until you notice what it cannot mean. Nobody speaks continuously. What he describes is closer to a line kept open — a running relationship rather than a scheduled event, where thanks and requests surface as the hours go.

Together they suggest something practical. Set aside a time small enough that you will genuinely keep it, and let the rest of the day stay open. The aim was never eloquence. It was contact, sustained.
lessons.lookCloser: Luke reports what the crowds were doing and what Jesus did. How are the two connected?
lessons.reflect: What would a small, sustainable prayer habit look like in your actual week?

studies.title: How to Use the Bible
studies.summary: How a Bible is arranged and how to find your way around one — references, cross-references, footnotes, and the tools in the back.
studies.audience: Anyone who owns a Bible and has never been shown how it actually works.

lessons.title: A library, and how it is arranged
lessons.understand:
Open the contents page before you open anything else. It is the most useful page in the book and the one almost everyone skips.

A Bible is a collection rather than a single work — dozens of separate writings, made across centuries, bound into one volume. How many depends on the edition: Protestant Bibles carry sixty-six, while Catholic and Orthodox editions include several more.

They fall into two parts. The Old Testament is the Scripture Jesus himself read and quoted. The New Testament was written after him, by people connected to him.

And they are not all the same kind of writing. Some are history, some poetry, some letters to particular churches, some visions. Reading a letter the way you would read a poem will mislead you, so it is worth knowing which one you are in — and the contents page, which groups them, is where that begins.
lessons.lookCloser: Find the contents page in your own Bible. How many books are listed before the New Testament starts?
lessons.reflect: Which kind of writing would you most like to understand better — a story, a letter, or a poem?

lessons.title: Finding a passage

rows.label: Book
rows.value: John — find it in the contents page

rows.label: Chapter
rows.value: 3 — the large numbers through the text

rows.label: Verse
rows.value: 16 — the small raised numbers inside the paragraph

lessons.understand:
Every reference is built the same way, and once you can see the pattern you can find anything.

The book comes first, then the chapter, then — after the colon — the verse. John 3:16 means the book of John, its third chapter, the sixteenth verse. Nothing else in the whole volume carries that address.

On the page the two numbers look different. Chapter numbers are large, usually set into the text or at the top of a column. Verse numbers are small and raised, sitting inside the paragraph where the sentence begins.

So finding a passage is mechanical. Look the book up in the contents, turn to the page, run down the large numbers to the chapter, then along the small ones to the verse.

Neither the chapters nor the verses were in the original writings. Both were added many centuries later, purely so that people could point at the same sentence — which is all they are for.
lessons.lookCloser: Find John 3:16 in your own Bible. Then find Matthew 5:3 without using the index, and notice how much quicker the second one is.
lessons.reflect: Is there a passage you have heard quoted for years and never actually looked up?

lessons.title: Reading a reference

rows.label: John 1:1-5
rows.value: A range. Verses 1 through 5 — what this lesson is showing.

rows.label: Romans 8:1, 28
rows.value: Two separate verses in the same chapter.

rows.label: Psalm 23
rows.value: A whole chapter. No verse given.

rows.label: 1 John 4:8
rows.value: The 1 belongs to the book name. Not a chapter.

lessons.understand:
References use a small set of marks, and each one means something exact.

A colon divides the chapter from the verse. A dash makes a range, so John 1:1-5 is five verses meant to be read together — which is what the card above is showing you. A comma separates verses that are not next to each other, so Romans 8:1, 28 points at two places in one chapter. A reference with no colon at all means the whole chapter.

One thing catches nearly everyone. Some books have a number in front of the name: 1 John, 2 Timothy, 1 Kings. That number is part of the title, not a chapter. There are three separate letters called John, and 1 John 4:8 sits in the first of them — a different book entirely from the Gospel of John.

When a reference will not come apart, read it left to right and stop at the colon. Everything before it names a place in the contents. Everything after it is a line on the page.
lessons.lookCloser: Look up 1 John 4:8, then John 4:8. Confirm for yourself that they are two different books in two different places.
lessons.reflect: Which of these marks had you been quietly guessing at until now?

lessons.title: Following a cross-reference
lessons.understand:
Most Bibles carry a quiet apparatus of connections. A small letter, number or symbol beside a word points to a list of other references — in the margin, in a narrow column down the centre of the page, or at the foot. These are cross-references, and they are the publisher saying: this sentence is related to those.

The two passages here are a real example. Peter, writing to scattered and pressured Christians, describes Jesus in language taken almost directly from a poem written centuries before him. Read them together and you can watch him reaching back on purpose.

Following one is also the quickest way to get out of your depth, so one habit protects you: when you arrive, read the paragraph, not only the verse you were sent to. A cross-reference points at a sentence without bringing its context along, and a line lifted out of a poem is not the poem.
lessons.lookCloser: Find 1 Peter 2:24 in your Bible and look for a marker beside it. Where does your edition keep its references — the margin, a centre column, or the foot of the page?
lessons.reflect: What might you miss by reading a linked verse without the paragraph it belongs to?

lessons.title: Headings, footnotes and marks
lessons.understand:
The most useful distinction in the book: some of what is printed is the text, and some was added to help you find your way.

Section headings — the short bold lines breaking a chapter into parts — are almost always the publisher’s. They are navigation, and another edition will word them differently or drop them. Useful, not Scripture, and quietly able to steer how you read what follows.

Psalms complicate that instructively. Many open with a line naming an author or a tune. Those lines are in the manuscripts, but editions disagree about how to show them: some as a heading, some numbered as verse 1, some not at all. One text, three layouts.

Footnotes usually do one of a few jobs: an alternative translation, a note that manuscripts differ, a more literal rendering, or a modern equivalent for a coin. The marks pointing to them vary between editions, so find your Bible’s key once.
lessons.lookCloser: Look at the very start of Psalm 23 in your Bible. Is there a line naming David — and is it a heading, numbered as verse 1, or missing?
lessons.reflect: Does knowing which words are the publisher’s change how much weight you give a heading?

lessons.title: The tools in the back

figure.heading: What may be in your edition

rows.label: Concordance
rows.value: An index of words, showing where each one appears.

rows.label: Maps
rows.value: Turns unfamiliar place names into distances you can see.

rows.label: Introductions
rows.value: A page before each book: who wrote it, to whom, and why.

lessons.understand:
Nehemiah describes a public reading where the text was read aloud and then explained, so that people understood it. That has been the pattern ever since: the words, and then help with the words.

A good deal of that help may already be in your hands. Many Bibles carry a concordance — an alphabetical index of words showing where each appears. If you half-remember a phrase, that is how you find it. Some include maps, which turn a list of strange place names into distances you can actually picture. Many put a short introduction before each book.

Not every edition has all of these, and a slim one may have none. It is worth five minutes finding out what yours contains.

A search box does the concordance’s job faster, and it is genuinely useful. What it cannot do is tell you which of forty results is the one that matters. That part is still reading.
lessons.lookCloser: Turn to the back of your Bible and list what you find. If there is a concordance, look up one word you are curious about.
lessons.reflect: Which of these would help most with the way you actually read?

lessons.title: Reading in context
lessons.understand:
The last verse here is quoted more than almost any other, and nearly always on its own. Read the two sentences in front of it and it says something more specific — and more useful.

Paul is writing from prison, thanking a church for a gift they sent him. What he says he has learned is contentment: in plenty and in hunger, with much and with nothing. The famous line is the conclusion of that thought. The strength being described is strength to be content in either condition, not a general assurance that effort will succeed.

Nothing in the verse changes. What changes is what it is about.

So the habit worth building is small. Before deciding what a verse means, read the paragraph it lives in. Then ask who was writing, to whom, and what they were dealing with — which is exactly what a book introduction will tell you in a page.
lessons.lookCloser: Read verses 11 and 12 on their own, then read verse 13 on its own. What does each version seem to be promising?
lessons.reflect: Is there a verse you have seen quoted alone that you would now like to look up properly?

lessons.title: A way to study a passage

rows.label: Observe
rows.value: What does it actually say? Read it twice before deciding anything.

rows.label: Understand
rows.value: Who wrote it, to whom, and what kind of writing is this?

rows.label: Connect
rows.value: What do the surrounding verses, or a cross-reference, add?

rows.label: Reflect
rows.value: What would this ask of someone who took it seriously?

rows.label: Apply
rows.value: One specific thing, held loosely — not a resolution.

lessons.understand:
Here is a method that works on any passage. It is not clever, and that is the point: most of the work is looking rather than deciding.

Take the psalm above. Observe first — it sets two ways of living against each other, and the opening line moves: walking, then standing, then sitting. Something is settling.

Then understand. This is poetry, and it is placed first in a collection of songs, which suggests it is an introduction to the whole book rather than a promise about outcomes.

Then connect. The picture is a tree by water, bearing fruit in its season — not immediately, and not constantly.

Only then reflect, and only then apply. Notice how late those come. Most disappointment with Bible reading starts at the last step: deciding what a passage means for today before working out what it said to anyone.
lessons.lookCloser: Try only the first step on the passage above. Write down three things it says, without interpreting any of them.
lessons.reflect: Which of the five steps do you usually skip?

studies.title: Foundations
studies.summary: The parts of a Bible and how to find anything in it: testaments, references, and what is text rather than trimming.
studies.audience: Anyone who has never been shown how the book is put together.

lessons.title: Two testaments, one volume
lessons.understand:
A Bible is bound as one book and works as two collections.

The Old Testament came first and is far the longer of the two. It is the Scripture Jesus grew up with, read aloud, and argued from — which is what this verse is describing him doing.

The New Testament was written afterwards by people connected to him: accounts of his life, letters to young churches, and a closing vision.

Knowing which half you are in tells you a great deal before you read a word. An Old Testament page is likely to be centuries before Jesus and addressed to Israel. A New Testament page is likely to be within a lifetime of him and addressed to scattered believers. Neither fact settles what a passage means, but both keep you from expecting the wrong thing.
lessons.lookCloser: Open your Bible roughly in the middle. Which testament did you land in — and how did you tell?
lessons.reflect: Which half of the Bible are you least familiar with?

checks.prompt: What is the Old Testament, in relation to Jesus?
options: The Scriptures Jesus himself read and quoted
The part written after Jesus by his followers
A summary of the New Testament for beginners
checks.explain: The Old Testament was already ancient in Jesus’ lifetime — it is what he read in synagogue and argued from. The New Testament is the part written after him.

checks.prompt: Someone tells you to read Habakkuk and you have no idea where it is. What is the fastest first move?
options: Look the name up in the contents page
Flip through the pages until the name appears
Start at Genesis and read forward until you reach it
checks.explain: The contents page lists every book with its page number, in the order they appear. It answers this in seconds, and it is the page most people never think to use.

lessons.title: The parts of a reference
lessons.understand:
A reference is an address, and it is written the same way every time: book, then chapter, then verse.

The colon is the hinge. Everything to its left tells you which book and which chapter; everything to its right tells you which sentence. Once you can see that, an unfamiliar reference stops being a code.

A few conventions are worth knowing straight away. A dash makes a range, so John 1:1-5 means five verses read together. A comma separates verses that are not adjacent. And a reference with no colon at all — Psalm 23 — means the whole chapter.

One more, because it catches everyone: a number in front of the name belongs to the title. 1 John is a different book from John, not its first chapter.
lessons.lookCloser: Find John 3:16, then find 1 John 3:16. They are different books, and the second one is much nearer the end.
lessons.reflect: Which part of a reference had you been unsure about?

checks.prompt: In the reference John 3:16, which part identifies the chapter?
options: John
checks.explain: John names the book, 3 the chapter, and 16 the verse. The chapter is always the number between the book name and the colon.

checks.prompt: A reference is written simply as Psalm 23, with no colon and no second number. What does it point to?
options: The whole of chapter 23
Verse 23 of the book of Psalms
The twenty-third book of the Bible
checks.explain: No colon means no particular verse was singled out, so the reference is to the entire chapter — all six verses of Psalm 23.

lessons.title: Text, and everything around it
lessons.understand:
A printed page carries more than the text. Some of what you see was added by the publisher to help you navigate, and telling the two apart is one of the most useful things a reader can learn.

Section headings — the short bold lines that break a chapter into parts — are almost always editorial. They are helpful, and they can quietly steer how you read what follows. A different edition will word them differently or leave them out.

Chapter and verse numbers were also added, many centuries after the writings themselves, so that people could point at the same sentence.

Psalms are the interesting exception. Many open with a line naming an author or a tune, and those lines are in the manuscripts — but editions disagree about whether to print them as a heading, number them as verse 1, or leave them out. So a heading is usually editorial, and occasionally it is not.
lessons.lookCloser: Look at Psalm 23 in your own Bible. Is there a line naming David, and is it a heading, a numbered verse, or absent?
lessons.reflect: Has a heading ever shaped what you expected a passage to say?

checks.prompt: Which of these was most likely added by the publisher rather than written by the biblical author?
options: A short bold line above the psalm summarising it
The sentence about a shepherd in the first verse
The name of the book at the top of the page
checks.explain: Summarising headings are editorial navigation and vary between editions. Book names and the text itself do not. It is worth noticing which is which before letting a heading frame your reading.

checks.prompt: You see a small raised letter beside a word in a verse. What does it most likely point to?
options: A footnote or a cross-reference elsewhere on the page
A printing error the publisher did not catch
The name of the translator of that verse
checks.explain: Small letters, numbers and symbols are the pointers into a Bible’s notes. Which mark means what varies by edition, so the key at the front is worth finding once.

lessons.title: What a cross-reference is for
lessons.understand:
Beside many verses you will find a marker leading to a short list of other references — in the margin, in a centre column, or at the foot of the page. Those are cross-references.

They are the publisher pointing out that this sentence is connected to those: the same idea, the same event, or in cases like this one, an older passage the writer was drawing on directly.

They are genuinely useful and they are not part of the text. Two editions will offer different lists, because deciding what counts as related is an editorial judgement.

And they carry one risk. A cross-reference sends you to a single verse, not to the paragraph it lives in — so it is very easy to arrive somewhere, read one line, and draw a conclusion the surrounding text would not support.
lessons.lookCloser: Find 1 Peter 2:24 in your Bible and look for a marker beside it. Where does your edition keep its references?
lessons.reflect: What is the appeal, and the danger, of reading by jumping between linked verses?

checks.prompt: You follow a cross-reference and arrive at a verse in another book. What is the best thing to do first?
options: Read the paragraph around it before drawing any conclusion
Read just that verse and go back where you came from
Follow the next cross-reference from this new verse
checks.explain: A cross-reference points at a sentence but does not bring its context along. Reading the paragraph is what stops a linked verse from meaning whatever it appears to mean on its own.

checks.prompt: Where do the cross-references in a Bible come from?
options: Editors, who chose which passages to connect
The biblical authors, who wrote them into the text
A standard list that is identical in every Bible
checks.explain: Cross-references are editorial. They are useful, they reflect real connections, and different editions offer different lists — which is worth remembering before treating one as decisive.

studies.title: Practice
studies.summary: Working with a passage: genre, the surrounding paragraph, comparing two texts, and what footnotes and search can and cannot do.
studies.audience: Anyone comfortable finding a verse who wants to read one better.

lessons.title: What kind of writing is this?
lessons.understand:
Before asking what a passage means, it is worth asking what sort of writing it is. The same sentence does different work in a law code, a letter and a poem.

This is poetry, and it works by picture. A person rooted in what God says is like a tree by water, bearing fruit in its season. That is an image of a settled and nourished life.

Read as a poem, the closing line about prospering describes that flourishing. Read as if it were a contract, it becomes a guarantee that plans will succeed — which the rest of the Bible, including several other psalms, plainly does not support.

Nothing about the words changed. What changed was the kind of writing they were assumed to be. Genre is not a technicality; it is the difference between those two readings.
lessons.lookCloser: Find the tree image in the passage above. What does it say about when fruit appears?
lessons.reflect: Which kind of writing do you find hardest to read well?

checks.prompt: Psalm 1 pictures a flourishing person as a tree by water. Read as poetry, what is that image doing?
options: Describing a settled, nourished life
Guaranteeing that any plan will succeed
Giving advice about where to plant trees
checks.explain: Poetry works by picture rather than by clause. The tree describes a kind of life; treating it as a contract turns a description into a promise the passage never makes.

checks.prompt: Which question is actually asking about genre?
options: Is this a poem, a letter, a law, or an account of events?
How long is this chapter?
Which translation am I reading?
checks.explain: Genre is the kind of writing. Length and translation matter for other reasons, but only the first question changes how the sentences are meant to be taken.

lessons.title: The paragraph is the unit
lessons.understand:
Verses are an addressing system, not a unit of thought. The unit of thought is the paragraph, and reading one verse without it is where most misreadings begin.

The last line here is quoted more than almost any other, usually alone. In front of it, Paul says what he has learned: contentment, in plenty and in hunger, with much and with nothing. He is writing from prison, thanking a church for a gift.

So the strength he describes is strength to be content in either condition. Read on its own, the same sentence sounds like an assurance that effort will succeed — a different claim, and not the one being made.

The habit is small and it costs nothing: read the paragraph before you decide what the verse is about.
lessons.lookCloser: Read verses 11 and 12 without the last verse. What has Paul actually said he learned?
lessons.reflect: What would change if you read a paragraph every time instead of a verse?

checks.prompt: Read with the two verses in front of it, what is the last verse of this passage mainly about?
options: Being content whether you have much or little
Succeeding at whatever you set out to do
Physical strength and endurance
checks.explain: Paul names the subject himself in the two verses before: he has learned contentment in plenty and in want. The famous line is the conclusion of that thought, not a separate promise.

checks.prompt: A verse on its own seems to promise something surprisingly large. What is the best next step?
options: Read the paragraph it sits in
Take it as it stands, since it is in the Bible
Look for a translation that phrases it more strongly
checks.explain: The paragraph is where the writer says what they are talking about. Shopping for a translation that agrees with a first impression is the opposite move — it protects the reading instead of testing it.

lessons.title: Holding two passages together
lessons.understand:
Sometimes two passages are obviously related, and the useful skill is saying carefully how.

Peter writes to Christians under pressure and describes Jesus in language that runs very close to a poem written centuries earlier. This is not coincidence: he is reaching back deliberately, applying older words to something he believes they anticipated.

Notice what that does and does not license. It is fair to say Peter is drawing on Isaiah. It is not fair to flatten the two into one statement and read whatever Peter means back into every line of the older poem, which was written into its own situation and has its own argument.

So compare them side by side, and keep asking what each one is doing where it stands.
lessons.lookCloser: Find the words the two passages share. Then find something present in one and absent from the other.
lessons.reflect: What is gained by reading two related passages together rather than either alone?

checks.prompt: Peter describes Jesus in wording very close to Isaiah 53. What is the most careful thing to say?
options: Peter is deliberately drawing on Isaiah’s language
Isaiah was quoting Peter
The resemblance is coincidence and means nothing
checks.explain: Isaiah was written centuries earlier, so the borrowing runs one way. Calling it deliberate is supported by how close the wording is; calling it coincidence ignores that.

checks.prompt: Two passages use similar words. Before concluding they mean the same thing, what should you check?
options: What each passage is talking about in its own context
Which one is longer
Which one comes first in the contents page
checks.explain: Shared vocabulary is a starting point, not a conclusion. The same word can do different work in two different arguments, and only the context of each shows which.

lessons.title: Notes, and what search cannot do
lessons.understand:
Luke describes a group who heard a startling claim and went and checked it against Scripture themselves. He calls them noble for it. Checking is treated here as a credit, not as doubt.

Two ordinary tools make that easier. Footnotes usually do one of a few jobs: offering an alternative translation, noting that manuscripts differ, giving a more literal rendering, or converting a coin or a measure. A note reading "Or:" followed by another word is telling you the original could reasonably be rendered either way — not that something is wrong.

Search, in a printed concordance or an app, finds occurrences fast. What it cannot do is judge them. Forty hits for one word will include several senses, several genres and several arguments, and sorting those out is still reading.
lessons.lookCloser: Find a footnote anywhere in your Bible. Which of those jobs is it doing?
lessons.reflect: When you have checked something for yourself, what changed?

checks.prompt: A footnote beside a word reads: "Or: covenant". What is it telling you?
options: The original word could reasonably be translated either way
The translators made a mistake in the main text
That verse is missing from some Bibles
checks.explain: An "Or" note offers a defensible alternative rendering. Notes about manuscripts differing are usually worded differently, and neither is an admission of error.

checks.prompt: You search a word and get forty results. What is the one thing the search has not done?
options: Judged which results are relevant to your question
Found the places the word occurs
Shown you the references
checks.explain: Search is very good at finding and very bad at weighing. The same word will appear across different genres and arguments, and deciding which occurrences bear on your question is the reading part.

studies.title: Deeper study
studies.summary: Reading with more care: observation before interpretation, where a passage sits, spotting a quotation, and testing an application.
studies.audience: Anyone who wants to check their own reading rather than trust a first impression.

lessons.title: Observation before interpretation
lessons.understand:
There are three different activities that often get done at once, and separating them improves everything afterwards.

Observation is what the text says. Here: the disciples wake him, they ask whether he cares that they are dying, he speaks to the wind, it stops, and afterwards they are more afraid than they were during the storm.

Interpretation is what it means — that the fear at the end is a response to him rather than to the weather, for instance. That is a reading, and a defensible one, but it is a step beyond the sentences.

Application is what to do about it, and it is the step most often taken first.

Doing them in order is not pedantry. Most confident misreadings are an interpretation that was never checked against an observation.
lessons.lookCloser: List three things the passage states plainly, without explaining any of them.
lessons.reflect: Which of the three do you tend to jump to first?

checks.prompt: Which of these is an observation about this passage, rather than an interpretation of it?
options: The disciples ask Jesus whether he cares that they are dying
The disciples had not yet understood who he was
This passage teaches us to stay calm in difficulty
checks.explain: The first is on the page in so many words. The second is a reading of what their question implies, and the third is an application. Both may be reasonable; neither is observation.

checks.prompt: Why is it worth doing observation before interpretation?
options: It settles what the text says before you decide what it means
It is faster than reading the passage closely
It removes the need to know the context
checks.explain: Observation gives interpretation something to be accountable to. Skipping it is how a confident reading ends up resting on something the passage never actually said.

lessons.title: Where a passage sits
lessons.understand:
Literary context is simply what comes before and after in the same book, and it is often the fastest way to understand a hard saying.

Immediately before this, Peter says out loud that Jesus is the Messiah — and Jesus responds by describing his own rejection and execution. Only then does he turn to the crowd and talk about taking up a cross.

That placement does real work. To people who had just heard him predict his own death, and who had seen crucifixions, the phrase was not a metaphor for inconvenience. It described a life no longer organised around self-protection.

Historical context adds the other half: knowing what a cross was to a first-century listener is not decoration, it is the difference between hearing the sentence and hearing something milder.
lessons.lookCloser: Read the verses just before this passage in your own Bible. What has just been said?
lessons.reflect: Has knowing what came before ever changed a passage for you?

checks.prompt: This saying comes straight after Jesus predicts his own rejection and death. What does that placement most affect?
options: What "take up his cross" would have meant to the people listening
Which chapter number the passage is given
Nothing — a verse means the same wherever it sits
checks.explain: The surrounding paragraph is what makes the phrase concrete rather than figurative. Placement is not decoration; it is part of how the sentence was meant to be heard.

checks.prompt: What does "literary context" refer to?
options: What comes immediately before and after, in the same book
The century in which the book was written
The translation you happen to be reading
checks.explain: Literary context is the surrounding text. When the book was written is historical context, and both help — but they are different questions with different answers.

lessons.title: Spotting a quotation
lessons.understand:
Biblical writers quote each other constantly, and noticing it opens a passage up.

Here Luke shows Jesus reading aloud from Isaiah, handing the scroll back, and saying the words have been fulfilled today. Recognising the quotation lets you go and read Isaiah for yourself and see what those lines originally announced.

It also lets you notice something sharper. Isaiah’s sentence continues past where the reading stops, into a clause about judgement. Luke’s citation ends before it.

That is an observation, not yet an interpretation — the text includes this much and not that much. What it means is a further question, and worth being careful about. But you cannot even ask it until you have noticed where the quotation ends.
lessons.lookCloser: Look up Isaiah 61:1-2 in your own Bible and read one line further than Luke does.
lessons.reflect: What does it change to know a writer is quoting rather than composing?

checks.prompt: Recognising that a passage is quoting an older one mainly lets you do what?
options: Go and read the older passage and see what it originally said
Skip the quoted section as already familiar
Treat the quoted words as more important than the rest
checks.explain: A quotation is a doorway. The writer expected the older passage to be in the reader’s mind, so reading it is part of reading them.

checks.prompt: You notice that a New Testament citation stops one clause short of where the Old Testament sentence ends. Noticing that is:
options: Observation — what is and is not on the page
Interpretation — deciding why the writer stopped there
Application — deciding what to do about it
checks.explain: Seeing where a quotation ends is observation. Explaining why it ends there is interpretation, and it is a further step that should be taken carefully and separately.

lessons.title: Testing an application
lessons.understand:
The last skill is the one that keeps the others honest: asking whether an application a passage is being used for is actually supported by it.

These words are addressed to people deported to Babylon, and the sentence immediately before names the timeframe — after seventy years. This is a promise to a nation about the end of an exile most of the original hearers would not live to see.

None of that makes it a smaller passage. It says something about how God treats a people he has not finished with, and Christians have long read it as revealing something about his character more widely.

What it will not carry is the weight often put on it: a personal guarantee that a particular plan will work out soon. Testing an application is not scepticism. It is asking the passage what it is prepared to say, and then saying that.
lessons.lookCloser: Read the verse before this promise. What timeframe does it name?
lessons.reflect: What is the difference between reading a passage carefully and reading it coldly?

checks.prompt: Who was this promise originally addressed to?
options: People taken into exile in Babylon
Individual readers making personal plans
The disciples, shortly before the crucifixion
checks.explain: The chapter opens by naming the audience: captives carried from Jerusalem to Babylon. The verse just before this one gives the timeframe — after seventy years.

checks.prompt: Which application does this passage most clearly support?
options: God keeps his intentions toward a people he has not abandoned
Any specific plan you are currently making will succeed
Difficult circumstances always end within a short time
checks.explain: The passage speaks about God’s posture toward a people across a seventy-year exile. The other two read a national and long-range promise as a short-range personal one, which is more than it says.
